title: A year after Takaichi's Taiwan remarks, China says Japan is 'entirely' to blame for the freeze
dek: Beijing's foreign ministry said Tokyo had 'not moved at all' since the Japanese prime minister linked a Taiwan crisis to Japan's survival; Tokyo again pointed to the 1972 joint communique and declined to retract.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China said on Friday that the "serious difficulties" in its relations with Japan were "entirely the responsibility of the Japanese side", as the two Asian powers marked a year since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told her parliament that a Chinese attempt to blockade Taiwan by force could threaten Japan's survival.

The Chinese foreign ministry's spokesman, Guo Jiakun, said at his regular briefing in Beijing that the Japanese government had "not moved at all" in the past year and had been "evading the issue". Japan's chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, said the same day that Tokyo's position on Taiwan "remains as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communique", restating an old formula rather than withdrawing the prime minister's words, which is what Beijing has demanded. Neither side announced any meeting between their leaders.

## What happened

Asked by Japanese reporters whether China would again call on Japan to withdraw the remarks, Mr Guo said they had been erroneous, had "blatantly signaled a potential military intervention in the Taiwan question" and had damaged the political foundation of relations, according to the ministry's transcript and a report by China's official news agency. He said Japan's "pressing priority" was to correct its "erroneous words and deeds on the Taiwan question", and that it should also adopt a correct attitude towards history and form "an objective and rational perception on China". China's position, he said, had been consistent.

In Tokyo, Mr Kihara told his regular press conference that China was an "important neighbor" and that Japan wanted a "constructive and stable relationship" through dialogue, according to reports. A senior foreign ministry official, Masaaki Kanai, director-general of the Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau, gave the same answer to the foreign affairs committee of the lower house of parliament on 28 October, reports said.

## Background

The dispute began on 7 November 2025, when Ms Takaichi, answering a question in a budget committee of the House of Representatives, said a Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan involving the use of force could amount to a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, according to reports. Under Japan's security laws, that is the legal condition that allows its Self-Defense Forces to use force alongside an ally even when Japan itself has not been attacked. Previous Japanese leaders had avoided saying what kind of Taiwan crisis would meet that test.

Beijing, which regards Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to take it, treated the remarks as a direct challenge. Since then, according to reports, it has:

- discouraged its citizens from travelling to Japan; reports describe the fall in Chinese visitors as a burden on Japan's economy
- cancelled screenings of Japanese animated films and concerts by Japanese singers in China
- tightened export controls on military "dual-use" items bound for Japan, including rare earths, in January 2026
- detained two employees of Japan's Fuji Electric group in the port city of Dalian in May 2026

There has been one public attempt to break the deadlock. In September, Takeshi Iwaya, a former Japanese foreign minister who was leading a private business delegation, proposed to China's foreign minister, Wang Yi, that both governments reaffirm the spirit of the 1972 communique, according to reports. Mr Wang did not accept, saying the issue could not be resolved "in an ambiguous manner", the same reports said.

In the 1972 communique, which established diplomatic relations, Japan said it "fully understands and respects" Beijing's position that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Tokyo says nothing in Ms Takaichi's remarks changed that position, and that whether a "survival-threatening situation" exists would be judged on all the information available at the time.

## What else China said

The same briefing showed how Beijing is handling its other big relationship. Asked about the United States, Mr Guo would not say whether China would delay a pledged $17 billion of American farm purchases until Washington implemented an agreed $30 billion-for-$30 billion reduction in tariffs, as China's commerce ministry has suggested. He referred the question to the "competent authorities" and said: "The two sides need to move in the same direction."

He also rejected new US sanctions on two Chinese companies accused of supplying Cuba's military, calling China's cooperation with Cuba "completely above-board", and said Beijing would take all necessary measures to protect Chinese firms. And he defended a court in Macao, which has sentenced a former legislator, Au Kam San, to 12 and a half years in prison for colluding with foreign forces, saying China opposed outside interference in such cases.

## Why it matters for India

Japan is one of India's closest strategic partners and a member, with India, the United States and Australia, of the Quad. This week an Indian frigate, INS Sahyadri, took part in the Malabar naval exercise with the three other Quad navies off Japan. A prolonged freeze between Tokyo and Beijing shapes the security climate in the waters through which much of the trade between India and East Asia passes.

The tools China has used against Japan are also familiar to New Delhi. India, like Japan, relies heavily on Chinese supplies of rare earths and the magnets made from them for its electronics, car and defence industries, and Beijing's decision to tighten export controls on one neighbour over a political dispute is a reminder of how that dependence can be used. Beijing's message to Tokyo, that relations will not improve until a leader's words on a sovereignty question are withdrawn, mirrors the terms on which it has dealt with other governments over Taiwan and Tibet.

## What happens next

Leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group are due to meet in Shenzhen, in southern China, on 18 November. It remains unclear whether Ms Takaichi and President Xi Jinping will hold talks there, according to reports. One report noted that US President Donald Trump is seeking his own deal with Beijing, which could leave Tokyo with less room to manoeuvre.

Neither government has signalled a change of position. China wants the remarks withdrawn; Japan says its policy has not changed and that it will not retract them.

## Timeline

- 7 November 2025: Ms Takaichi tells a parliamentary committee a forcible blockade of Taiwan could be a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan
- January 2026: China tightens export controls on dual-use items, including rare earths, bound for Japan
- May 2026: two Fuji Electric group employees detained in Dalian
- September 2026: Wang Yi turns down a proposal to reaffirm the 1972 communique
- 6 November 2026: China says Japan has "not moved at all"; Japan restates the 1972 position
- 18 November 2026: APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen
